opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it started from my own pain. Around the time I was getting ready to go to the US for grad school, I needed to book a visa appointment, and the slots at the consulates in China were really hard to get. The official site only let you check one location at a time, and the earliest available date kept changing. So everyone was refreshing the page over and over, and people were sharing screenshots in WeChat groups, like "Beijing just opened something in two weeks!" It was chaotic and very inefficient.

I thought, this is a simple automation problem. Have a script check the dates periodically for all the cities, record them, and show everything in one place, maybe with a little history so you can see trends. So I wrote a small crawler for myself, and then figured that if it was useful to me, it would probably help a lot of other students in the same situation. I put it online, and it spread much faster than I expected, especially later when COVID hit and consulates were closing and reopening unpredictably. Many people relied on it to decide when and where to apply.

There was also a bit of the "why not" spirit. I liked building small tools that solve real problems, and I had the skills to do it, so it felt natural to just build it rather than complain. Later other people contributed too, and it became more of a community project. It taught me that something technically quite simple can have a big impact if it hits a real need.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the visa-date tool began with Jiayi’s own difficulty booking an appointment and that other students faced the same problem. It does not identify Tianshou or connect those needs to building it.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it started out of pure frustration. Back in 2020, when the pandemic hit, I was a Chinese student in the US on an F-1 visa, and like a lot of people in my situation, I needed to get my visa renewed before I could travel. But consulates were shutting down, slots were disappearing, and the official appointment system was basically a black box. You'd log in, click through five or six pages, and finally see "no appointments available," and then you'd do it again an hour later because someone might have cancelled.

I was doing that manually, refreshing the page over and over, and at some point I thought, this is ridiculous. I'm a programmer. This is exactly the kind of repetitive, mechanical task a script should handle. So I wrote a little crawler that would check the available dates for me and ping me when something opened up.

Then I realized I wasn't the only one. Friends were asking me to check for them, people in WeChat groups were posting screenshots of dates they'd found, and all that information was scattered and out of date within minutes. So I thought, why not just put it online? Put the data on a page, let anyone look at it, and later add things like email or push notifications so people don't have to stare at a screen all day.

tuixue.online was already a side project I'd been running, mostly for fun, so hosting it there was natural. The visa page kind of took over though. It went from a personal tool to something that tens of thousands of people were checking daily during the worst of the appointment shortage.

I think the deeper reason I built it myself rather than waiting for someone else is that I have this instinct that if a problem is annoying enough and you have the skills to fix it, you should. It's the same mindset I had with Tianshou, the reinforcement learning library: I was tired of existing tools being slow or awkward, so I just built the thing I wanted. The visa system was the same idea applied to a very different kind of pain.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes building the visa tool to solve Jiayi’s own frustrating appointment-search problem and says Tianshou came from being tired of existing tools, calling both the same idea applied to different problems.
